newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico stocks sharply down on Dow jitters.
newsitem.headline: Mexico stocks sharply down on Dow jitters.

text.p: Mexican stocks extended an early fall to trade sharply lower mid-morning on Monday.
Dealers said a thin volume market was swayed as investor caution over the Dow Jones ahead of Tuesday's Fed meeting outweighed strong domestic GDP figures.

"People are not so aggressive on the buy side after Friday's fall on the Dow, and didn't want to go long into the weekend," said Michael Gould, head of sales trading at the Latinvest brokerage in New York.
The leading IPC share index was down 65.13 points, or 1.31 percent, at 4,891.48.

The Dow Jones recovered from an early fall this morning to rise 3.02 points to 7,697.68. But dealers were quick to note the industrial average had suffered its second biggest point slide ever on Friday, which outstripped the fall on the IPC that same day.

Dealers said concerns over the Dow Jones outweighed the impact of stronger-than-expected GDP data and news Finance Minister Guillermo Ortiz's brother was killed in what police say was an attempted robbery on Saturday.
"It (the killing) is certainly a serious issue, but it will not derail an economy this strong," Gould added.

The Finance Ministry announced Mexico's GDP gained 8.8 percent during the second quarter of the year compared to year-ago data. This was appreciably higher than the average 5.92 percent increase predicted in a Reuters survey.

Alejandro Ortiz, brother of Minister Guillermo Ortiz, was shot and killed on Saturday evening. Dealers said players were concerned the slaying may have been politically motivated, though no evidence for this has emerged so far.
Floor traders noted volume, at just 16.1 million shares, was very thin and showed just how cautious the market was.
"More than anything it's lack of buyers, no way is it a sell-off," one trader said.
Financial group Bancomer, one of Mexico's biggest, was the most traded stock and had declined 6 centavos to 5.18 pesos on market jitters, dealers said.
Mexican TV network TV Azteca shares were off 20 centavos to 36.60 pesos. Dealers said the share had "cooled down" as market enthusiasm had waned since the firm went public on Friday.
On the broad market, decliners far outnumbered gainers, by 55 to 10, out of 82 stocks traded.
"Friday's fall on the Dow Jones had a delayed effect on the bourse today, but we also recovered due to the Dow and today's strong GDP figures," a floor trader said.
The Dow Jones, meanwhile, rebounded from a low of 7,618.47 points to end up 108.70 points at 7,803.36.
The Finance Ministry announced shortly before trade opened that Mexican GDP rose 8.8 percent in the second quarter from the same quarter last year.
Dealers said market caution was clearly visible in wafer- thin trading volume of 56.7 million shares, itself inflated by a cross trade of 7.5 million shares.

Traders said dealing had also slowed on news Alejandro Ortiz, Finance Minister Guillermo Ortiz's brother, was shot and killed on Saturday evening. Police said they were investigating a robbery, although no valuables were taken from Ortiz.

"We didn't see it drive the market, but we did get many calls from concerned foreign investors asking what was going on," a floor trader said. Market heavyweight Telefonos de Mexico did most to haul the bourse out of its early slump, ending up 18 centavos at 20.00 pesos. The telecom's ADRs ended up 1/4 at 51-9/16.

Dealers noted television network TV Azteca, which went public on Friday, recovered from an earlier slump to close unchanged at 36.80 pesos in relatively brisk trade. The stock still ended above its floatation price of 35.43 pesos.
Traders said media group Televisa and construction firm Empresas ICA weighed most on the market. Televisa ended off 4.80 pesos at 123.20, while ICA declined 30 centavos to 23.80 pesos.
On the broad market, losses outnumbered gains by 68 to 22 out of 118 stocks that changed hands.
(( --Elena Vega, Mexico City newsroom +525 728-7901))
